# Results — Study 368 (Buyback-Drift)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The folklore — **a stock drifts
up for months after it announces a big share-buyback authorization** — tested as a clean event
study on **abnormal** (stock − SPY) returns. We time the **authorization** (the board/press
release OK of a $X program — what the headline reacts to), explicitly **not** execution (actual
repurchases trickle out over years). The sample is a hard-coded, transparent table of **32**
notable mega-cap authorizations; the inference is a one-sample t plus a **same-names placebo
null**. Offline & deterministic given the cache; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce
every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — SPY + 32 event tickers (public, no key) |
| As-of | **2026-06-18** (last cached bar; pull ≤ 2026-06-22) |
| Window | 2010-01-04 → 2026-06-18 (**4,140** trading days) |
| Event sample | **32** hard-coded notable buyback **authorizations** (ticker, announce date, $bn size); an explicit, **named SAMPLE** (point-in-time authorization feeds are not free) |
| Measure | **abnormal** forward return = (stock_T/stock_0 − 1) − (SPY_T/SPY_0 − 1) |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag (trade the close *after* the announcement); 10 bps round-trip on a single-name hold |

> **Sample caveat (named on the Signal axis).** The table is hand-picked mega-cap
> authorizations — selected on **visibility** and on the firm having **survived**, both
> upward-biasing. It also enters **one day after** the announcement, so it deliberately
> **excludes the announcement-day jump** (a real, documented ~2–3% pop) and measures only the
> *subsequent drift* — which is what the "drifts up for months" claim is actually about. The
> verdict does not hinge on the exact 32 names: it hinges on the fact that *any* few-dozen
> single-name event set is dominated by single-stock variance, which holds a fortiori for the
> true population (which includes the small, unglamorous programs the headlines skip).

## The signal — abnormal drift after each authorization vs zero

1-day entry lag. The abnormal return strips SPY, so this is drift *beyond the market*. The
one-sample Welch *t* tests the mean against **0**; the placebo *p* is the share of 20,000
same-names random-date draws whose mean abnormal return **beats** the announcement set.

| horizon | n events | abn. mean | abn. median | win-rate | Welch *t* (vs 0) | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-month  | 32 | **+0.52%** | +0.67% | 59% | **+0.72** | 0.392 |
| 3-month  | 32 | **+2.42%** | +0.91% | 53% | **+1.19** | 0.200 |
| 6-month  | 32 | **+4.49%** | +1.12% | 56% | **+1.21** | 0.165 |
| 12-month | 32 | **+5.34%** | +1.69% | 53% | **+0.87** | 0.338 |

Read it carefully. The mean abnormal drift is **positive at every horizon** — exactly the
direction the folklore predicts, and consistent with the *sign* of the academic
underreaction literature. But **no horizon clears the t ≥ 2 bar** (the best is *t* = 1.21 at
6 months), the **medians are far below the means** (a few big winners pull the average up —
the typical event drifts ~1%), and the placebo says a same-names random-date draw matches or
beats the announcement set **17–39%** of the time. The win-rate sits near the **50%**
single-name coin-flip. This is a positive-but-insignificant point estimate dominated by
single-stock variance — not a certifiable edge.

## Costs barely move it — which is itself the point

| horizon | n trades | gross abn. mean | net @ 10 bps round-trip |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-month  | 32 | +0.52% | +0.42% |
| 3-month  | 32 | +2.42% | +2.32% |
| 6-month  | 32 | +4.49% | +4.39% |

A 10-bps single-name round-trip shaves ~0.1pp off a multi-month hold — costs are **not** the
binding constraint. The binding constraint is **statistical power**: a mean drift inside its
own standard error is not a strategy regardless of the per-trade number.

## Robustness — split by program size (does "bigger buyback ⇒ bigger drift" hold?)

| bucket | n | abn. 6m mean | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| BIG (≥ median $20.4bn) | 16 | +2.81% | 0.52 | 0.612 |
| SMALL (< median) | 16 | +6.17% | 1.19 | 0.042 |

The "bigger program ⇒ bigger drift" prediction **fails outright** — the *bigger*
authorizations drift *less* (t = 0.52). The SMALL bucket's 6-month placebo *p* = 0.042 looks
tempting, but it is a **median-split multiple-testing fluke**: its *t* is only **1.19** (well
under 2) and the same bucket gives *t* = −0.67 / 0.60 / 0.53 at 1 / 3 / 12 months. Slice a
32-event set into two and one half *will* look good by luck — the textbook reason a single
sub-bucket p-value is not an edge.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and ~30 events are weak

On a deterministic panel of **31 event windows** with a **known planted abnormal drift**
injected over the 6-month window, the inference behaves exactly as it should:

| planted 6m drift | detected | abn. 6m mean | Welch *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no edge) | 31 | +2.62% | 0.66 |
| **+0.15** (large edge) | 31 | +10.61% | **2.47** |

With **no** planted drift the test does **not** cross t = 2 (it cannot manufacture
significance from ~30 noisy windows, even when the draws tilt the point estimate to +2.6%).
Only a **huge** planted drift — +15% abnormal over six months — drives *t* to 2.47. The
control proves two things at once: the measurement engine is unbiased, **and** ~30 single-name
events is too few to detect any drift of plausible magnitude. That is the entire lesson.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The drift is positive at every horizon (the folklore and the academic
  underreaction story agree on the *sign*), but it **fails the t ≥ 2 bar at every horizon**
  (best t = 1.21), the median event drifts ~1%, the win-rate ≈ a coin-flip, and the
  same-names placebo can't reject luck. Literature support + a positive-but-insignificant
  point estimate ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL. **Survivorship + visibility selection** in the
  hand-picked table is named here on the Signal axis.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs are negligible (10 bps off a months-long single-name hold),
  but the per-trade abnormal drift is **inside its own error bar**, the typical (median) event
  barely moves, and "bigger buyback ⇒ bigger drift" is *false*. A drift you can't distinguish
  from zero on 32 events is **not a NAV-scale strategy**.
- **"Free lunch"? — BUSTED.** "Announce a buyback, the stock drifts up for months" is a
  **base-rate + small-sample mirage**: enter *after* the documented announcement-day pop, strip
  the market, and what's left is a positive-but-noise drift that a same-names coin-flip matches
  ~1 time in 5. The announcement-day *jump* is real; the tradable *months-long drift after it*
  is not certified.
